title: Open work, live state and conflicts
summary:
This part settles what happens to everything that exists before the rewrite starts: what counts as production, the legacy freeze, the live hosts and services, the nine draft PRs, defects found while mining, the lead and repository access, cleanup, stale agent guidance and automation, the June decision records and Linear. End states that other parts decide (scope, hosting, legacy domains and repositories, releases, generated agent docs, the style-injection fix, the delivery gates) are referenced by item ID, not decided twice; this part decides dispositions, timing and order. The last group, Cross-part contradictions, is the exception: where parts propose incompatible answers, it decides which one holds. Item IDs stay as first published because other parts cite them: OPN-23 was withdrawn because INT-50 decides the rewrite's repository and history, OPN-43 to OPN-49 were added in review, and OPN-50 to OPN-68 come from the cross-part consistency pass.

Items that need Daniel's judgement:

- Production and the freeze (answered): production is the Worker version richview.ai serves, built from #69's branch, and `prod` records it once #69 is merged as it stands (OPN-01, OPN-13). No legacy hotfix ships: the live site was never advertised, so it changes when the rewrite reaches `prod`, and its defects become rewrite fixtures (OPN-02, OPN-43, FEA-SF-30; OPN-17 to OPN-20).
- Live hosts (answered, done on 27 Oct after Daniel's go): the workers.dev copy of the site is hidden behind Cloudflare Access as the `dev` preview, richview.uk and its app and docs subdomains return 301 to richview.ai, the v2 API record is gone, and both Fly apps are destroyed after backups (OPN-44, OPN-04, OPN-45, OPN-05).
- News: publishing has been out of service since 2026-10-19; the RichView News session repairs it on PR #70, and News, one instance of Publish, moves onto the rewrite's Publish once that can serve it (OPN-03, OPN-46, INT-74).
- October automation: the paused supervisor, its standing deploy authority and the executor delegations in Linear were retired (OPN-47, answered and done on 27 Oct).
- People (answered): Daniel leads RichView alone. "Steven" was an agent persona, not a person, so no one is told or invited and nothing waits on him (OPN-48, OPN-24), and the repositories he appeared to co-own were archived (OPN-25, done on 27 Oct).
- Cross-part contradictions: nineteen choices on which two or more parts propose incompatible answers, from the performance gate and the prod receipt to style settings, diagnostic codes and the part 05 types; each card names its sides by item ID and proposes the rule that settles them (OPN-50 to OPN-68). Every cited card points back to its contradiction card under conflicts.

Housekeeping Daniel can accept in bulk once those are answered: the PR dispositions (OPN-06 to OPN-12, OPN-14: #62, #63, #65, #66, #67 and #68 are closed unmerged and their features enter the rewrite (FEA-BR-01, FEA-BR-08, OPN-63); #64 leaves the repository (INT-34); #70 is merged into `main` as it is (INT-35, INT-52), and its JavaScript retires once News moves onto the rewrite's Publish), worktree residue (OPN-15), the legacy defects (OPN-16, OPN-21, OPN-22), the old organization, URLs, prerelease and branches (OPN-26 to OPN-29), stale guidance (OPN-30 to OPN-34, OPN-49), the June decision records (OPN-35 to OPN-40), Linear (OPN-41) and unclarified dictation (OPN-42). The style-file script injection waits for the rewrite because no deployed host renders another author's style file on a real origin; the VS Code preview runs it in its webview (OPN-16).

How to answer: accept keeps the proposal as written and becomes the chief of staff's instruction for repository, branch, Linear and local-machine work; anything that changes a live site, a public repository or DNS, revokes or creates a credential, spends money, or sends an invitation or message still waits for Daniel's explicit go at the time. Edit rewrites the proposal, reject drops it and defer leaves it open. Where this part and a referenced item disagree (noted under conflicts), answer the referenced item first. The cross-part contradiction cards reverse that order: answer each before the cards it cites, which then follow it. Confidence `observed` means re-checked on 2026-10-21 or 2026-10-22 against b4db233, the live sites, GitHub, Linear or the operator machine.

items.title: Legacy code is frozen except one bounded hotfix
items.question: Does the legacy product keep receiving work while the rewrite is built, and what may the one exception fix?
items.why: Parallel work on legacy code produced three deploys from unmerged branches, duplicate fixes and five conflicting PR pairs in one week; every legacy change competes with the rewrite for agent time and for Daniel's review. Yet the live site breaks on phones, links dead pages and states what part 01 rules out until launch (INT-39, INT-41, INT-42, INT-65), and part 04c hands those corrections to this item (FEA-SF-30, FEA-SF-45).
items.proposed: Until the rewrite reaches `prod`, legacy code takes no feature or design work and no hotfix: the live site was never advertised, so it changes only when the rewrite reaches `prod` (FEA-SF-30). Its layout defects, dead links, status labels and false statements stay live until then, and each becomes a rewrite fixture or check (OPN-17 to OPN-20, OPN-22, OPN-43). Any later legacy fix needs Daniel's explicit authorization and follows DEL-65. Under Daniel's DEL-02 answer no frozen `main` remains: the legacy state is the commit `main` holds when it is renamed `prod`, a fix Daniel authorizes starts from a new branch off that commit, and how such a fix reaches richview.ai while only `dev` merges into `prod` is open (DEL-65). The update signup on richview.ai and its D1 subscriber data stay untouched (INT-72). The reel's one render for posts changes no deployed code (FEA-SF-45, OPN-64).

The publisher's last cycles failed because the gateway's sync returned 503 on 2026-10-18 and 502 on 2026-10-19, and the publisher has been disabled since Daniel paused all RichView services on 2026-10-20. The transfer presumably adds a second break: the gateway and publisher name the old repository and refuse GitHub's redirect. According to #70's docs, urgent hide and rollback work without GitHub, so a takedown path remains (stated). Daniel decided on 2026-10-23 that News is not frozen and is being improved now on PR #70 (INT-74); a repair needs a new credential and a production deploy, both on his go.
items.proposed: The RichView News session repairs News publishing as part of its work on #70's code, merged into `main` as it is on 2026-10-26 (INT-35, INT-52): the bridge reads 1vecera/richview (or a content repository of its own, ARC-16) with a new repository-scoped credential, and the desk and editor login work again. Each News deployment happens on Daniel's go. The lockdown neither freezes nor takes down News. News is one instance of Publish, which the rewrite rebuilds (INT-31, INT-35): when the rewrite's Publish can serve it, a deployment from `prod` replaces this one on Daniel's go (INT-74, DEL-40), with its own repository-scoped credential (OPN-46).

items.question: What happens to the disabled News publisher on Claw Mini and to the GitHub credential the News bridge holds, now that News is being improved?
items.why: The publisher's launch agent is disabled but still installed with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive, so re-enabling it restarts a job pointed at the old repository. The News Worker holds a GitHub credential as its `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret, which the repaired publishing path needs again, scoped to the new repository (OPN-03).

Each of these outward steps happens on Daniel's go. When News moves onto the rewrite's Publish (INT-31, INT-74), the #70 publisher job is removed and its credential revoked once the new deployment publishes, again on Daniel's go; the rewrite's Publish holds its own credential under ARC-23.

items.why: #70 is Publish's first implementation (about 4,000 lines of JavaScript gateway and editor, 1,000 lines of Rust), live from its branch until Daniel's INT-35 answer merged it into `main` on 2026-10-26 (merge commit 97ac0d0). His INT-31 answer builds Publish in the rewrite and makes News one instance of it, and his INT-52 answer merges #70 as it is, so the News work lands and continues, while the rewrite carries over what Publish strives for, not its code.
items.proposed: #70 is merged into `main` as it is, JavaScript included, on 2026-10-26, so the RichView News session's work lands and continues there (INT-35, INT-52, INT-74). It is not the rewrite's base: the rewrite builds Publish on the new core and the server core it shares with Cowork (INT-31, INT-35, ARC-57) and carries over what Publish strives for, its behaviour and decisions, not its code; #70's JavaScript is ported to the Rust target when the rewrite reaches Publish (INT-49, INT-52). Its spec stays recorded in FEA-BR-23 to FEA-BR-30, FEA-BR-44 to FEA-BR-46 and FEA-BR-49, with TYP-80 and TYP-81 for its formats, as requirements of the rewrite's Publish. When the rewrite's Publish can serve News, News moves onto it as its first instance with its content migrated (INT-51), and #70's JavaScript gateway and desk retire. With `main` renamed `prod` (DEL-02), #70's code is part of the state `prod` and `dev` start from (OPN-01). Open: which branch News deploys from now that #70's branch is fully merged (DEL-40's table, which Daniel's answer keeps for News, still names it and `publish/news`), how ARC-03's allowlist check treats #70's JavaScript until the port, and when News cuts over.

items.title: Per-batch performance follows part 07: no load wait, WebKit in the full capture
items.question: Does every release run (a batch merged from `dev` into `pre-prod`, DEL-81) run every performance budget and a WebKit probe after waiting for a quiet host (DEL-08, DEL-51, DEL-62, DEL-43), or part 07's smaller per-batch set without a wait, with WebKit and the other budgets in the full capture (PRF-02, PRF-04, PRF-24)? A merge into `dev` runs the fast gate only (DEL-81).
items.why: Parts 02 and 07 describe two different performance steps for the same gate run, written for a gate on every merge into `dev` (`rv-gate dev`). Daniel's DEL-81 answer limits a `dev` merge to the fast gate, unit tests ideally under five seconds, and puts the long suites on the combined state at release, so the question moves to the release run. DEL-51 waits for a 1-minute load average of 2.0 or less, checks every budget and adds a WebKit probe. PRF-02 replaces the wait with a lock and an outside-CPU check, PRF-04 keeps about 4 minutes of budgets and moves WebKit, the phone profile, PDF export time, memory sessions and builds to a full capture, and PRF-24 times WebKit only there and on motion PRs. Accepting both sides makes the gate wait and not wait. The answer sets how long a release takes and how many agents can work at once on Claw Mini.
items.proposed: A merge into `dev` runs no performance budget: its fast gate is unit tests only (DEL-81). The release run, which merges a batch from `dev` into `pre-prod`, runs part 07's set (PRF-04) for what the batch affects under PRF-02's lock and outside-CPU check, without waiting for a load average. WebKit timing runs in the full capture, daily on a changed `pre-prod` head and at each prod candidate, and on batches that change motion (PRF-24); the phone profile, PDF export time, memory sessions, build durations and absolute millisecond limits run only in the full capture. DEL-08's registry row and DEL-51 drop the load wait and the per-merge WebKit probe; DEL-62 has no agent cap beyond DEL-81's two Opus agents, and the chief of staff lowers the number of heavy streams when PRF-02's "performance inconclusive" recurs; DEL-43 has no merge lock, so a capture holds only PRF-02's host lock.

options.label: Every budget per release after a load wait (DEL-08, DEL-51, DEL-62, DEL-43)
options.detail: Strictest per release. Releases wait for a load average Claw Mini rarely reached in the captures so far (1.8 to 7.3), so agent work must be capped, and every release pays for a WebKit probe. Measured 157.2 s for today's harness, run per merge; the wait and the probe are not measured.

options.label: Per-batch set without a wait (PRF-02, PRF-04, PRF-24)
options.detail: About 4 minutes per release by estimate, judged against interleaved base runs, so a busy host slows a capture without changing its verdict. A regression in WebKit timing, the phone profile, PDF export time or memory is found by the next daily capture and bisected to its batch.

items.recommendation: Per-batch set without a wait (PRF-02, PRF-04, PRF-24): under DEL-81 agents merge into `dev` on the fast gate alone and the release run is what proves a batch, so a load threshold the host rarely meets would stall releases and with them every agent behind them; only Daniel's `prod` merge needs the full evidence, which the full capture still provides.

items.title: Connectors: none in the core; a secondary path owned by RichView Publish
items.question: Where do live data connectors belong now that Daniel's INT-24 answer makes them a secondary path of RichView Publish, and what becomes of PR #66's contract (ARC-59, OPN-10, TYP-79, FEA-BR-14 to FEA-BR-16, FEA-BR-43)?
items.why: Daniel's INT-24 answer (2026-10-26) keeps exported data the default for every report and puts live connections in RichView Publish, served by an existing third-party connector engine so RichView does not build connectors itself. ARC-59, OPN-10, TYP-79, FEA-BR-14 to FEA-BR-16 and FEA-BR-43 had recorded PR #66's own SQL, MetricFlow and snapshot adapters as a later-phase option inside RichView's native host. They disagree on where connectors live and who builds them; the core and Publish, both built in the rewrite (INT-31, INT-35, ARC-57), need one owner.
items.proposed:
RichView Publish owns live data connectors; the core builds none. Publish is built in the rewrite (INT-31, INT-35), so the connector path attaches to the rewrite's Publish on the new core, not to #70's JavaScript Worker stack. A report rendered by the CLI from its folder reads only data exported into that folder (TYP-35, FEA-RP-41) and never makes a live query; the core format and `richview-app` gain no connector code. In Publish, a CMS-style publishing setup can serve stories from live data as a secondary path, and its connectors come from an existing third-party connector engine, not from RichView-built adapters. Cowork may later store data-source credentials, such as SQL credentials, so its reports read live data the same way; not in its first cut (INT-83). Whether the connector path then sits in the server core Cowork and Publish share is open. The Publish host holds every data-source credential in its own configuration; credentials never appear in `.rmd` files, styles, report folders, rendered output, MCP tool arguments or agent context (ARC-23), and the secret scan covers them (DEL-55). PR #66's contract (ARC-59, TYP-79, FEA-BR-14 to FEA-BR-16, FEA-BR-43) stays recorded as requirements for that path and its DuckDB and MetricFlow adapters as one option, not the plan.

Open question for Daniel, to choose later: which third-party connector engine Publish uses. Candidates, not researched: dlt, Airbyte or PyAirbyte, DuckDB extensions, Steampipe, Cube, MetricFlow. Also open: whether the connector path lands in Publish's first cut or after News runs on the rewrite's Publish (INT-74).
